Alfozan also used an AI tool meant for OpenAI employees to find internal documentation about executives visiting Saudi Arabia and which OpenAI officials were most likely to attend meetings with Saudi ministers, according to a court filing. Alfozan was in regular contact with a Saudi royal who tried to recruit him for a new AI venture launching in Saudi Arabia. Lawyers for Alfozan did not respond to a request for comment.
Some employees have long been concerned about the wide availability of information within OpenAI, the five people familiar with OpenAI's practices said.

Anybody at OpenAI who could access its code could also see the details underlying many of the company's projects, including sensitive ones unrelated to an employee's work. That is because OpenAI stored most of its code in a single repository, known in the industry as a "monorepo," the people said. The monorepo was dense and complicated, which may have deterred some would-be attackers in the past. Now, AI agents can sift through that amount of material.

In the past, OpenAI has kept much of its research documentation on GitHub and Slack, raising concerns among some employees that motivated actors could still find crucial information, the five people said. But one of the sources and OpenAI said the company has restricted access to sensitive work.

OpenAI emphasised that much of its most sensitive work is held in separate code repositories with strict access controls. And it said the monorepo does not contain all of its code or critical details of the company’s models, including the numerical values that determine how a model behaves, known as the model weights.

Another issue is that OpenAI had not done regular security reviews of its internal tools, such as the so-called sandboxes where researchers stress-test new models, three people familiar with the company’s practices said. Employees often modified those tools for their work, but those changes were not always tested for security problems, leaving them potentially vulnerable to attacks from outsiders, the three people said.

The company said it has a strong approach to security under its chief information security officer, Dane Stuckey, who joined in October 2024. OpenAI said it now conducts regular security reviews of its internal tooling.
Open debate versus security
OpenAI is not the only AI company to face security problems.

In January, a federal jury in San Francisco convicted a former Google employee who was arrested in March 2024 on charges of stealing thousands of pages of confidential information about Google's AI technology on behalf of China.

In late October, a cybersecurity startup called Cathedral Systems said it hacked into Anthropic's systems and gained access to Slack channels where employees discussed sensitive model details. An Anthropic spokesperson said the data accessed included some business contact information for customers and partners as well as a set of basic user account records. Cathedral's CEO did not respond to a request for comment.

OpenAI and Anthropic have tried to maintain a more open research culture to both attract employees and foster creativity that can lead to breakthroughs. The AI field is rooted in academia, where machine-learning scientists have openly discussed their research.
Some OpenAI employees are increasingly worried about this approach as AI grows more capable, according to the five people.

In 2023, Leopold Aschenbrenner, then an OpenAI researcher, wrote an internal memo titled “OpenAI is China’s leading AI lab” about his concerns that China could infiltrate OpenAI and study its technology, three people familiar with the matter said.

Aschenbrenner shared that memo with some board members later that year after an outsider hacked into OpenAI and took details about its GPT-4 model. OpenAI said the hacker accessed only Slack channels available to the whole company.

Security concerns within OpenAI flared up again this summer when OpenAI agents being tested hacked into the AI company Hugging Face, an incident that prompted scrutiny from state, local and federal officials, including the White House.

Cybersecurity firm Hacktron AI said three of its researchers used a rival AI model from Anthropic in July to break into ChatGPT accounts belonging to multiple OpenAI employees and gained access to some internal OpenAI systems, including its monorepo. The incident exposed how advanced AI can now put the AI companies themselves at risk of attack.
OpenAI's Widmann said the company thanked the researchers for sharing their findings and that it took steps to minimise the risk of similar attacks in the future.
After Reuters sought comment for this story, OpenAI said on Monday in a blog post that it is planning its "next internal security sprint" to beef up its defences.

headline: Milo Ventimiglia recalls filming 'Gilmore Girls' while dating Alexis Bledel
subheadline: The 'This Is Us' alum dated the 'Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants' actress from 2003 to 2006
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Milo Ventimiglia is looking back fondly on his time with Gilmore Girls and his real-life romance with costar Alexis Bledel.

In an interview with Us Weekly published Tuesday, November 3, the 49-year-old actor reflected on filming the beloved series, recalling the memories he made with Bledel and fellow star Jared Padalecki.

Ventimiglia joined the Amy Sherman-Palladino drama in its second season as Jess Mariano, Rory Gilmore’s troubled boyfriend.

READ MORE: Milo Ventimiglia says he's okay with his daughter being Team Dean

“The episodes are for an audience to pick apart, dissect,” he said. “For us to make it, [it’s] the experience of making it. What were those days like on set? Hanging out with Jared Padalecki, being with [costar and real-life love] [Alexis [Bledel]]. The experience is something that I always lean into, that really fills me up.”

One particular memory involved filming on the Warner Bros. backlot with Bledel. Ventimiglia recalled insisting that a prop bag be weighted to make it look convincingly heavy.

Ventimiglia and Bledel dated for three-and-a-half years before splitting in 2006. Bledel previously revealed that the couple had discussed marriage.

READ MORE: 'Gilmore Girls' gets first official behind-the-scenes documentary

headline: Chris Rock takes responsibility for divorce in candid interview
subheadline: Chris Rock opens up about therapy, divorce and Oscars slap
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Chris Rock has opened up about going to therapy, saying he sought help because his personal life was not where he wanted it to be.

The comedian made the remarks in a candid GQ interview, published on Tuesday as part of the magazine’s Men of the Year honours.

“My personal life wasn’t what I wanted it to be,” Rock said. He recalled going into therapy “crying like a b**ch,” but declined to share more about what was discussed.

Read more: Chris Rock's daughter Zahra to join him in 'Grown Ups 3'

Rock also took responsibility for the end of his marriage to Malaak Compton-Rock, which lasted 19 years.

“I was not a great husband,” he said, adding that he “watched a lot of po*n.” He said he has not watched it for “five, six years.”

On the Oscar slap, the star kept his answer short.

“Something happened. It wasn’t cool,” he said, making clear that he would like to move on. He wants attention to be on his work, he explained, rather than on “some crazy night.”

There is plenty of work to talk about.

His film Misty Green arrived in cinemas via A24 last month and will be available on Netflix on 9 November. Rock also said he plans to direct more feature films, write a book and possibly return to the stage.

The GQ cover is the first of the magazine’s Men of the Year honorees to be unveiled this year, and it sees one of the biggest names in stand-up reflecting openly on the personal changes he has been through.

Read more: Chris Rock on Will Smith slap: 'I wish nothing would have happened'

headline: US midterms enter decisive phase as polls begin closing, Trump faces tough challenge
subheadline: Democrats are favoured to capture the House and could also win the Senate, curbing President's Trump's power
author: AFP
article_text:
Economic discontent, high energy costs, Iran war weigh on Republicans.
More than 57m voted early, with campaign advertising topping $11b.
NY voting machine malfunctions fuelled unfounded fraud claims.

Polls began closing Tuesday in US midterms with Democrats poised to seize the House and potentially the Senate, threatening to shatter Donald Trump's grip on Washington and curtail his power for the rest of his presidency.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Trump's legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.

The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump at a time when the mood is turning sharply against Republicans over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats were at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.

As the first polls began closing in Kentucky and Indiana, House Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in Washington that the country was "on the brink of a dramatic change of direction."

"We're on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives," he predicted.

Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict that he launched have squeezed Americans.

The 80-year-old's approval rating has hovered near the low 30s, making him one of the most unpopular presidents in history.

Taylor Cook, a Los Angeles voter, told AFP that affordability and reining in the Trump administration were the two biggest election issues.

"Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing, and I want people in Congress who will actually do something about costs," the 24-year-old said.

Economic discontent

Trump defended his record in a final TV phone-in pitch to voters on Tuesday, saying he had rebuilt the country through his immigration crackdown, war on Iran and tariffs.

"We have to keep America great. We're great now. We were terrible two years ago," Trump told "Fox & Friends."

Republicans insist that Trump's tax cuts and anti-migrant stance will benefit voters, and they have portrayed Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals -- a message that has seemed to resonate with some voters.

"Democrats used to be decent in the past but they became very socialist," Maru Restrepo, a 70-year-old voter of Colombian origin, told AFP in Miami.

Trump has campaigned to help Republicans, but polls show he may have weighed them down instead.

In his final public appearance on Monday, Trump barely touched on the election and gave a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington's Reflecting Pool.

"He's done everything that was needed. Republicans are in a better spot now than they were four weeks ago," a White House official told AFP.

But Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded Trump's final speech "pathetic."

Disputed results?

The Senate is a steep hill for Democrats to climb.

While Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the angry mood had extended the battlefield into once reliably conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

But Democrats must defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

Decision Desk HQ's final forecast projected 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.

The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, and mega-rich Trump ally Elon Musk has poured nearly half a billion dollars into Republican efforts.

Concerns were high that Republicans -- especially Trump -- will refuse to accept results if they lose.

Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats -- with no evidence -- of cheating.

Voting machines malfunctioned in a hotly contested House race in New York state on Tuesday, prompting right-wing influencers to fling unfounded allegations of fraud even as local election officials insisted all ballots would be counted.

article_html:
• Economic discontent, high energy costs, Iran war weigh on Republicans.
  • More than 57m voted early, with campaign advertising topping $11b.
  • NY voting machine malfunctions fuelled unfounded fraud claims.

Polls began closing Tuesday in US midterms with Democrats poised to seize the House and potentially the Senate, threatening to shatter Donald Trump's grip on Washington and curtail his power for the rest of his presidency.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Trump's legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.

The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump at a time when the mood is turning sharply against Republicans over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats were at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.

As the first polls began closing in Kentucky and Indiana, House Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in Washington that the country was "on the brink of a dramatic change of direction."

"We're on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives," he predicted.

Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict that he launched have squeezed Americans.

The 80-year-old's approval rating has hovered near the low 30s, making him one of the most unpopular presidents in history.

Taylor Cook, a Los Angeles voter, told AFP that affordability and reining in the Trump administration were the two biggest election issues.

"Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing, and I want people in Congress who will actually do something about costs," the 24-year-old said.

Economic discontent

Trump defended his record in a final TV phone-in pitch to voters on Tuesday, saying he had rebuilt the country through his immigration crackdown, war on Iran and tariffs.

"We have to keep America great. We're great now. We were terrible two years ago," Trump told "Fox & Friends."

Republicans insist that Trump's tax cuts and anti-migrant stance will benefit voters, and they have portrayed Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals -- a message that has seemed to resonate with some voters.

"Democrats used to be decent in the past but they became very socialist," Maru Restrepo, a 70-year-old voter of Colombian origin, told AFP in Miami.

Trump has campaigned to help Republicans, but polls show he may have weighed them down instead.

In his final public appearance on Monday, Trump barely touched on the election and gave a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington's Reflecting Pool.

"He's done everything that was needed. Republicans are in a better spot now than they were four weeks ago," a White House official told AFP.

But Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded Trump's final speech "pathetic."

Disputed results?

The Senate is a steep hill for Democrats to climb.

While Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the angry mood had extended the battlefield into once reliably conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

But Democrats must defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

Decision Desk HQ's final forecast projected 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.

The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, and mega-rich Trump ally Elon Musk has poured nearly half a billion dollars into Republican efforts.

Concerns were high that Republicans -- especially Trump -- will refuse to accept results if they lose.

Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats -- with no evidence -- of cheating.

Voting machines malfunctioned in a hotly contested House race in New York state on Tuesday, prompting right-wing influencers to fling unfounded allegations of fraud even as local election officials insisted all ballots would be counted.

headline: Pakistan's financial inclusion reaches 71%, gender gap narrows to 27%: SBP governor
subheadline: Climate finance must extend beyond green investments to help vulnerable communities withstand risks: Ahmad
author: Web Desk
article_text:
SBP, Alliance for Financial Inclusion inaugurate 4-day programme.
Programme brings together 38 central bank reps, officials from 24 states.
Pakistan shares its Green Taxonomy, climate risk framework with members.

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan's financial inclusion rate has reached 71%, while the gender gap has narrowed to 27%, State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) Governor Jameel Ahmad said on Tuesday, stressing the need to extend climate finance to women, smallholder farmers and small businesses.

Addressing the inaugural session of a four-day joint learning programme organised by the SBP and the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI) in Islamabad, Ahmad said climate change and financial exclusion were closely linked, with communities most exposed to climate risks often having the least access to insurance, savings and formal financial services.

"Climate finance must do more than support green investments. It must also help communities anticipate risks, build resilience and adapt to a changing climate," he said.

The programme has brought together 38 representatives of central banks and financial regulators from 24 countries across four continents. It aims to help participating institutions translate inclusive green finance policies into practical measures and strengthen climate-resilient financial systems. The programme is being held in Pakistan for the first time.

Ahmad cited the devastating 2022 floods as an example of the economic and social costs of climate-related disasters. The floods caused nearly $15 billion in physical damage and a further $15 billion in economic losses, affected more than 30 million people and damaged 2.2 million homes.

He said the scale of the losses underscored the need for financial systems that were both environmentally sustainable and inclusive.

The governor said Pakistan was sharing its Green Taxonomy and climate risk framework with regulators across the AFI network. He outlined the SBP's measures to integrate environmental considerations into the financial sector, including the Green Banking Guidelines issued in 2017, the Environmental and Social Risk Management Framework introduced in 2022, the Pakistan Green Taxonomy and regulations on climate-related financial risks.

He also referred to the Climate Stress Testing Guidelines issued in December 2025, which help financial institutions assess their exposure to climate-related shocks.

On women's access to finance, Ahmad highlighted the Pakistan Women Inclusive Finance Programme, supported by the Asian Development Bank. He also noted that Pakistan joined the Women Entrepreneurs Finance Code in 2025, with the SBP serving as the anchor institution for the financial industry.

The governor outlined Pakistan's work under AFI's four pillars of Promotion, Provision, Protection and Prevention. These include classifying environmentally sustainable economic activities, directing financing towards underserved groups, strengthening women's financial resilience and preparing financial institutions to manage climate-related risks.

He said participants would exchange experiences on implementing inclusive green finance policies, supporting climate-smart agriculture and addressing barriers to implementation, including those related to gender.

"The success of any policy framework is ultimately measured by its implementation and its impact on people's lives," he said.

AFI Director of Strategy, Member Engagement and Evaluation Aban Haq and World Bank Operations Manager Lasse Melgaard also addressed the inaugural session, highlighting the importance of international cooperation and knowledge-sharing in promoting inclusive and sustainable finance.

He outlined the SBP's measures to integrate environmental considerations into the financial sector, including the Green Banking Guidelines issued in 2017, the Environmental and Social Risk Management Framework introduced in 2022, the Pakistan Green Taxonomy and regulations on climate-related financial risks.
He also referred to the Climate Stress Testing Guidelines issued in December 2025, which help financial institutions assess their exposure to climate-related shocks.

On women's access to finance, Ahmad highlighted the Pakistan Women Inclusive Finance Programme, supported by the Asian Development Bank. He also noted that Pakistan joined the Women Entrepreneurs Finance Code in 2025, with the SBP serving as the anchor institution for the financial industry.

The governor outlined Pakistan's work under AFI's four pillars of Promotion, Provision, Protection and Prevention. These include classifying environmentally sustainable economic activities, directing financing towards underserved groups, strengthening women's financial resilience and preparing financial institutions to manage climate-related risks.

He said participants would exchange experiences on implementing inclusive green finance policies, supporting climate-smart agriculture and addressing barriers to implementation, including those related to gender.
"The success of any policy framework is ultimately measured by its implementation and its impact on people's lives," he said.

AFI Director of Strategy, Member Engagement and Evaluation Aban Haq and World Bank Operations Manager Lasse Melgaard also addressed the inaugural session, highlighting the importance of international cooperation and knowledge-sharing in promoting inclusive and sustainable finance.

headline: Josh O'Connor reacts to James Bond speculation
subheadline: Next James Bond: Josh O’Connor says 'there is nothing to say'
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Josh O’Connor has described being linked to the role of James Bond as a “bizarre pinch me moment”, while former 007 Pierce Brosnan has offered warm words for rival contender Callum Turner.

O’Connor spoke to the BBC on Tuesday at the opening of the Everyman Theatre’s new education and community centre in his hometown of Cheltenham.

“To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary,” he said.

Read more: Is Sydney Sweeney the next James Bond girl?

The actor is reportedly among the candidates to replace Daniel Craig, alongside Turner and Jack Lowden.

He did not say whether he had taken part in any auditions. “There is nothing to say beyond that,” he said.

Brosnan, who played Bond in four films between 1995 and 2002, told Vanity Fair that he is now just “the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history.”

Of Turner, he said: “Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong.”

The two worked together on The Only Living Boy in New York in 2017. Brosnan added that all the men on the current list are “actors I admire.”

He also praised director Denis Villeneuve, calling him “such an iconoclastic director” and predicting that “we are going to be blown away.”

The untitled film is in development, with Steven Knight writing, Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing, and Villeneuve directing.

Pascal has told Deadline that she expects a casting announcement by the end of the year. Turner and Lowden are reported to be the frontrunners.

O’Connor won an Emmy for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and has since appeared in films including The Mastermind and The History of Sound.

Read more: ‘Slow Horses' Jack Lowden finally addresses his role in 'James Bond'

headline: Peter Phillips' wife Harriet shares biggest change since joining royal family
subheadline: Harriet Phillips credits Peter for helping her navigate new life
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Peter Phillips' wife Harriet has spoken about adjusting to life as a member of the royal family following her marriage to Peter Phillips.

The former NHS paediatric nurse married Princess Anne’s son in June after years spent balancing her career with raising her daughter.

Despite the changes that have come with her marriage, Harriet is determined to stay grounded and hold on to the values instilled in her from an early age.

Speaking to HELLO!, she explained how her upbringing had helped her remain true to herself, saying: "Hopefully, having my feet firmly on the ground beforehand is the most important thing.

If you've been through tricky things, you learn who you are and you don't get lost."

She was quick to credit Peter for making the transition easier, admitting that while royal life is unfamiliar territory for her, it is something her husband has always known.

"Peter really helps; he's grounding, because this is his normal. This is not my normal," she said.

Harriet also praised her parents for giving her a "wholesome, stable upbringing.”

Harriet described building a life with Peter as one of the most rewarding adjustments since their marriage.

"The biggest one is having a new shape of a family.

I'm now married and that’s a pleasurable adjustment, because it’s so lovely having somebody to share life and experiences with.

And trying to fit everything in!" she told the publication.

She admitted that juggling full-time work and motherhood had previously been a challenge, but she is now finding ways to create a better balance.

"Peter and I are so fortunate to have such wonderful girls between us.

I’m excited about what’s to come with our family and always mindful that going gently is so important," she said.

Harriet also revealed that she has already found someone she feels comfortable turning to for advice.

Asked about her first meeting with the Princess of Wales, she spoke warmly of her, saying: "I can look to Catherine for advice and guidance.

headline: Prince William, George share rare reunion in Spain wearing Remembrance poppies
subheadline: Fans can't get over Prince George's grown-up look during football night with William
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prince William finally enjoyed a special father-son night out with Prince George at Barcelona clash.

On Tuesday night, the father and son arrived Spain to cheer on their beloved Aston Villa as they took on FC Barcelona.

The appearance was particularly notable for George, marking his first public outing since starting at Eton College in September.

Read More: Prince William grabs British actor by shoulders in surprising nightclub clash

The 12-year-old appeared to be growing up fast, with royal watchers quick to notice how much taller and more mature he looked beside his father.

Both William and George showed their support for Remembrance Day by wearing poppy pins on their jackets.

Eton College is currently closed until Sunday, November 8, giving George time away from his studies for the trip.

Before kick-off, Barcelona president Joan Laporta greeted the royal guests and presented them with a personalised Barça shirt.

The VIP box also included former Barcelona goalkeepers Amador Lorenzo, Pere Valentí Mora and Jesús Mariano Angoy, alongside former club player Allan Simonsen.

Also seated behind William and George was Edward van Cutsem, the King's godson.

FC later acknowledged the Prince of Wales's attendance in a post on social media, thanking him for joining the club for the much-anticipated fixture.

FC later acknowledged the Prince of Wales's attendance in a post on social media, thanking him for joining the club for the much-anticipated fixture.

headline: Christina Applegate feels like 'fraud' after MS misdiagnosis
subheadline: Christina Applegate reflects on Multiple Sclerosis misdiagnosis
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Christina Applegate has said she feels like a “fraud” after learning she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, admitting she is “back at square one” in understanding her health.

The Dead to Me star, 54, spoke on her podcast MeSsy, which she co-hosts with Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

On the latest episode, recorded with guest Jack Osbourne, she joked: “Talk about being a fraud, I don’t even have it anymore, jeez.”

Read more: Christina Applegate feels she's 'let everybody down' after MS misdiagnosis

Applegate first revealed the misdiagnosis on the 20 October episode, saying she felt she had “let everybody down.”

She said she lived as a person with MS for almost six years, having announced her diagnosis in August 2021 while filming the third and final series of Dead to Me.

She has stressed that the news does not mean everything is resolved.

“This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one,” she said. She added: “You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I’m better.”

Applegate is now being tested for conditions with similar symptoms, including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and Lyme disease.

“So now I’m being tested for all that stuff, slowly but surely,” she said. No results have been shared.

She said the situation has left her more frustrated than relieved, and that she is still adjusting to this change in her health journey.

She also wants to stay involved in the MS community. “I’m still always going to be a part of it,” she said.

Osbourne, 45, who lives with MS, said he sometimes feels like a fraud himself, though his condition “hasn’t stopped me”.

Sigler, also 45, made Applegate an “honorary member” of the MS community, and Osbourne offered to send her some resources, which she said she appreciated.

Read more: Christina Applegate speaks out after 'misdiagnosed'

headline: King Charles reveals special island-inspired setting for royal dinner
subheadline: Royal watchers await for King Charles and Queen Camilla’s grand arrival
author: Web Desk
article_text:
King Charles and Queen Camilla are preparing to welcome Commonwealth leaders to a dinner in Antigua.

The Royal Family shared a BTS look at the preparations, sharing photographs of the beautifully arranged tables ahead of Tuesday evening’s official of Government dinner.

The table setting was a blend of island charm and royal tradition, with colourful checked tablecloths and napkins, floral arrangements and candle lanterns bringing warmth to the tables.

Palm trees and a sweeping coastal view provided a beautiful backdrop for the occasion.

Royal editor Rebecca English was equally taken with the preparations, sharing her own preview of the evening with followers.

"What a night! A preview of tonight's dinner thrown by the King features breathtaking Caribbean produce with a Buckingham Palace twist," she wrote.

She also noticed the locally made table mats, created by Antiguan artisan 'Sexy Sue', and a special cocktail named 'Commonwealth 56' – a nod to the organisation's 56 member countries.

headline: US midterms: Ossoff defeats rival to retain key Georgia Senate seat for Democrats
subheadline: A Democratic Senate majority would give the party greater power to scrutinise Trump's administration
author: Reuters
article_text:
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won reelection in Georgia on Tuesday, according to media projections, defeating President Donald Trump-backed Republican US Representative Mike Collins and preserving a crucial seat as Democrats seek to regain control of the Senate.

Ossoff's victory in one of the country's most closely contested Senate races marks an important win for Democrats in a state Trump carried by two percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

It also keeps the party's hopes of securing a Senate majority alive as results come in from across the country.

The senator, widely viewed as a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, raised $126 million more than Collins during the campaign.

Collins, meanwhile, benefited from $18 million in outside spending after emerging from a three-way Republican primary and subsequent runoff.

Trump had endorsed Collins over former college football coach Derek Dooley, who had the backing of outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp.

Republicans entered Tuesday's elections with a 53-47 majority in the Senate, meaning Democrats needed a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.

Georgia was among the seats Democrats had to defend to have a realistic chance of achieving that goal.

Their path also depended on retaining a seat in Michigan and defeating Republican incumbents in Maine and North Carolina, while making further gains in states Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024, including Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and Texas.

A Democratic Senate majority would give the party greater influence over legislation and the confirmation of senior government appointments, while making it harder for Trump to advance his agenda during the remainder of his presidency.
